title: NRI Tax Filing: When to File ITR After Moving Abroad
description: Becoming a Non-Resident Indian (NRI) does not automatically end your tax obligations in India. Your residential status for tax purposes is crucial and differs.

faq.q: ### Do I need to file an ITR if all my Indian income is from NRE accounts?
faq.a: No, interest earned on NRE (Non-Resident External) accounts is fully exempt from tax in India. Therefore, if your only income from India is from NRE accounts, you typically do not need to file an ITR.

faq.q: ### What is the difference between NRE and NRO accounts for tax purposes?
faq.a: Interest earned on NRE accounts is tax-exempt in India, while interest earned on NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) accounts is taxable in India. NRE accounts are for repatriable foreign earnings, whereas NRO accounts are for managing income earned in India.

faq.q: ### Can I claim deductions like Section 80C as an NRI?
faq.a: Yes, NRIs can claim certain deductions under Chapter VI-A of the Income Tax Act, such as Section 80C (for investments in PPF, ELSS, life insurance premiums, etc.), 80D (health insurance), and 80G (donations), provided the investments or expenses are made in India.

faq.q: ### What if I have a PAN card but no taxable income in India?
faq.a: Even if you have a PAN card but no taxable income, you are not mandated to file an ITR. However, as discussed, filing can be beneficial for claiming TDS refunds or carrying forward losses. Your PAN remains active regardless.

faq.q: ### Does my residential status change every year?
faq.a: Yes, your residential status for tax purposes is determined for each financial year independently, based on your physical presence in India during that specific year. It can change from Resident to NRI and vice-versa.

faq.q: ### What is a DTAA and how does it help NRIs?
faq.a: A Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) is a tax treaty between India and another country that prevents taxpayers from paying taxes on the same income in both countries. It helps by providing relief through exemption or tax credit methods, or by specifying lower tax rates.
